The meditation on the sixteen Subrahmaṇyās;
the twenty-five divisions of the forms of Maheśvara;
the Jātakaśiromaṇi. (p. 5a) (f. 3b)
Skanda, the wielder of the power of knowledge, likewise the commander of the divine army,
Subrahmaṇya, mounted upon an elephant, born from the forest of Śara reeds.
Kārttikeya, Kumāra, the six-faced one, the destroyer of Tāraka,
the general, the teacher of Brahmā, and the beautiful one, auspicious like a creeper.
Bāla, Cakrauñcabhoktṛ, and Śikhivāhana—
these sixteen names of the Lord a man [should recite] every day.
O Great Sage, whoever recites this shall be liberated from all sins.
Now, the names of the meditations corresponding to these [deities] are being declared. (1)

I worship the wielder of the spear, who has one face and two arms, holding a vajra in his left hand and [the spear] in his right, and who is the embodiment of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. (2)

I praise Skanda, the son of Kātyāyanī, who possesses two arms and one face, whose complexion is as red as a lotus, who is free from ailment, and who holds a staff and a loincloth tied at the waist in his right hand; he is Śaktidhara, the Lord, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree for those who bow before him. (3)
With a face like the moon, reddish-brown as the Sindhu river, adorned with divine ornaments such as armlets and necklaces, bestowing the bliss of heaven;
holding a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, a spear, and a cock, and radiant with red unguents.
We worship Subrahmaṇya, who is ever-ready to dispel the fear of those who bow before him.
(4) We worship Subrahmaṇya, who has one face, two arms, and holds the gesture of fearlessness bound at his waist; he resembles the young, reddish dawn. (5)

I perpetually bow to the Son of Īśvara, who has one face and two eyes, who holds an excellent cock in his two left hands and a sharp spear and the gesture of fearlessness in the other two; he possesses the splendor of ten thousand suns and rides upon an elephant for the sake of the attainment of desired goals—O Lord who rides the elephant! 6.

I meditate upon the six-faced one born from the forest of Śara reeds, who is yellow and gentle, possesses twenty eyes, and is the son of Kekaya; who bears a spear, a bell, a banner, a lotus, a cock, a noose, a staff, an axe, an arrow, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and a bow; who is worshipped by hosts of gods and revered by the virtuous, and who restrains both [the mind and the senses].

(7) And [I meditate on him] holding in his three left hands the gesture of granting boons, a thunderbolt, and a shield, and in another three [hands] the gesture of fearlessness, a spear, and a discus. (4)

I bow to Kārttikeya, who possesses the radiance of the rising sun, who is worshipped by the virtuous, and whose face is like a lotus. (8) I meditate upon Kumāra, the Lord of the Creeper, who holds a sharp spear and a sword in his two right hands, and a bell and a cock in his two left hands;
he whose eyes are wide and full like the moon, and who is ever intent on bestowing auspiciousness. (9)

I salute the one with the luster of vermilion, born from the forest of Śara reeds, seated upon a majestic peacock, the six-faced one, the beloved of Devasenā and the daughter of Madhuripu, who has twelve eyes, and who holds in his right hands a spear, an arrow, a sword, a banner, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness.

Wielding a bow, a thunderbolt, a lotus, an excellent bracelet, and a trident in his other hands; (p.7b) (f.6a) holding a boon-granting gesture, a goad, a banner, a bracelet, a bow, a thunderbolt, as well as the gestures of fearlessness, a noose, a wheel, a sword, a mace, and a spear in his twenty arms—worship here the Enemy of Tāraka, who resembles ten million suns and is the cause of the destruction of worldly existence. (ll. 2) 11.

I praise the Commander of the Divine Army, who holds in his twelve hands on both sides the *abhaya* [gesture], the sword, the goad, the spear, the trident, the *varada* [gesture], the thunderbolt, the noose, the lotus-stalk, and the mace; he possesses twenty eyes like lotuses.

(12) And in his pair of left hands he holds the excellent *kuṇḍikā* [water-pot] and the *viśākha* [staff], while in his right hands he holds the *akṣasūtra* [rosary] and the *abhaya* [gesture]. (p. 8a, f. 6b)
We pay homage to the one whose face is like the lotus of the forest, who is adorned with ten million creepers, and who is the teacher born from the lotus;

(l. 2) who holds a rosary and the gesture of fearlessness in his two hands, and a water-pot at his waist; who is seated upon the left [thigh], joined by the one summoned according to the prescribed rite held in the right hand. (l. 3)

I take refuge in Him who is adorned with every ornament, held by Viṣṇu bearing a water-pot, possessing a beautiful luster, whose form is auspicious like a creeper, and who is being praised by all the hosts of gods. 14.

I bow to the Son of Īśvara, who delights the young, who has one face, whose left hand rests upon his lotus-like right hip, who resembles the luster of a lotus, and whose arms are raised like those of a child. He has one face, two eyes, and two hands holding two lotuses.
I salute him who acts for the pleasure of the Brahmins, who has the form of a youth and the brilliance of the sun.

(15) I praise the destroyer of Krauñca, the leader of the celestial army, who possesses eight arms and six lotus-like faces; he holds in his right hands the sword of fearlessness, the spear, and the arrow, while in his other hands he carries the boon-granting gesture, the thunderbolt, the bow, and the shield. (16)

I bow to the one born of Rudra, who has the luster of coral, whose face is single, who is all-pervading, whose hands hold the thunderbolt, the spear, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness; he is the slayer of the enemies of the world of the gods, the bestower of freedom from obstacles, and has the peacock as his vehicle.

(17) [I bow] to the god who resembles the *ḍāḍīmī* flower, who has the hue of *guñjā* seeds, the brilliance of saffron, six faces, is accompanied [by his consort], possesses twelve eyes, and is in the full bloom of youth. (2)

One should always worship Kumāra, the son of Śaṅkara, who possesses four arms, is tranquil, is endowed with a sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*), and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; who is radiant with a crown and a casket-shaped head-ornament (*karaṇḍa*); who is adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and a girdle; who is possessed of all auspicious marks (*sarvalakṣaṇa*); who is accompanied by the great goddess Valli and Devasenā; who is beloved by the hosts of gods; and who brings about the welfare of all the worlds. 18. (l. 4)
Piṅgala, with Subrahmaṇya as his companion. (p.9b) (f.2a) 7.
May this Gaṇeśa named Ucchiṣṭa protect me—he who holds a blue lotus, a pomegranate, a lute, a cluster of rice, and a rosary. (8) (l. 2)
May Vināyaka, the Lord of All, who holds a noose and a goad, whose vehicle is a rat, who possesses breasts and bestows boons, and who is red in color, destroy all obstacles. 9. (l. 3)
One should meditate upon Kṣipragaṇādhipa, who has tusks like those of Gaṇapati, holds a noose and a jewel-pitcher that shine with a goad, and possesses the lovely luster of a bandhūka flower. (10)
Heramba-Gaṇapati,
with hands granting fearlessness and boons, holding a noose, a tusk, a rosary,
a staff (paraśu), a conch, a skull-cup, a mallet, and a sweetmeat (modaka), is seated upon a crouching lion.
May Gaṇapati named Heramba, who has the face of a five-tusked elephant and is the color of a young deer, protect [us]. (p. 10a) (f.
2b) Lakṣmī-Gaṇapati, who bears a parrot, a citron, a lotus, a ruby-pitcher, and a goad; (l. 2)

May the dark-complexioned [Viṣṇu], who holds a noose and a lotus in his hands, together with the goddess Lakṣmī—who is fair-limbed and whose lotus-hand bestows boons—protect you along with the hosts of deities. 12. (4)
Mahāgaṇapati, bearing a kalhāra flower, a water-pot, a goad, a tusk,
and a sugarcane arrow, together with a jewel-jar, a lotus, a noose, and a discus; (verse 5)

May the great Gaṇeśa, whose body is crimson and who stands near his Lord together with the Goddess, fair-limbed and with hand extended in the gesture of granting boons, bestow upon you eternal auspiciousness. 13.

Victorious is Vighneśvara, golden-hued like refined gold, his beauty enhanced by ornaments held in his hands: the conch, sugarcane bow, arrow, shield, axe, noose, discus, goad, pen, and inkpot; (verse 14).

I bow to Gaṇeśa, who stands in a single posture while dancing beneath the Kalpa tree; his shimmering hands hold a dance, a noose, a goad, a cake, and an axe as teeth, with their excellent fingers gracefully positioned; he possesses a yellow radiance. 15.

O Lord of the Upper Gaṇas, you whose tusk is the axe-weapon, whose body shines with the golden sprouts of the *kalhāra* and *śālikiṇi* trees, and whose hand is raised to embrace the body of the goddess—may that Lord of the Upper Gaṇas protect you from fear. 16. (p.11a, f.3b)
May the Vināyakas— namely Bāla, Taruṇa, Bhaktagaṇapa, Vīra, Śaktidvaja, Piṅgalarūpa, the Gaṇapa who precedes [the others], and the other named Ucchiṣṭa—
protect the splendor; and after them, may Herambaka quickly [grant it].
Then Lakṣmīśa, Mahāgaṇapati, Vighneśa, and Nṛttidhvaja. (L. 4) The meditation on the sixteen Gaṇapatis is complete.
[One should meditate upon] the divine Gaṇa, the Great Lord, who holds a goad and has four arms. (L. 5)
And likewise Mahādeva, who holds a noose and a goad...
Having a body consisting of twenty-five divisions:
the first should hold the moon; the second is joined with Umā;
the third is mounted upon a bull; and the fourth has the form of a dancer.
One should know the fifth to be the marriage [constellation], and the sixth is the wandering for alms;
one should know the seventh to be the maker (Kārī), and the eighth is the enemy of time (Kālāri).
The ninth is Tripurārī, followed by Jalandharavadha;
the eleventh is Gajarī, and the twelfth is Vīrabhadra.
The thirteenth is Keśavārtha; the fourteenth is Ardhanārī;
the fifteenth is Kirāta; the sixteenth would be Kaṅkāla;
and likewise, the seventeenth would be Caṇḍeśānugraha.

The removal of poison is likewise remembered as the eighteenth. The nature of the gift of the discus (*cakradāna*) is the nineteenth, and the propitiation of obstacles (*vighnaprasāda*) is the twentieth; after that follows the *Somāskanda*.
The twenty-second is the Single-Legged [posture], while the twenty-third is the Comfortable Seat (sukhāsana).
The twenty-fourth is proclaimed to be the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The nature of the Liṅgodbhava is traditionally known as the twenty-fifth;
these forms of Maheśa are proclaimed to be the various manifestations of Śakti.
(Verse 3) [This is] the meditation on Candraśekhara.

I praise the one who bears the crescent moon, whose limbs resemble the rays of the dawn, who has three eyes, and who holds an axe and a deer in his right hands; who embraces the Śakti with his left hand;

who is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons; who is adorned with necklaces and armlets; who wears bracelets on both arms; and who possesses the very form of the bearer of the Soma. (1) [This is the meditation upon him accompanied by Umā.]

One should worship in the heart [the Lord] who is white-complexioned, seated on a comfortable throne, endowed with power, holding a deer, an axe, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; who has a beautiful face, holds a blue lotus in his hand, and bestows boons, accompanied by Umā.
The meditation on the one mounted upon the bull:
the three-eyed deity stands upon the bull, his right arm resplendent with a thunderbolt; his left leg is placed upon the back of another [beast], while his right foot is slightly bent.
Standing with feet even, he holds an axe and a deer in his right hands, and a noose in his left; the god resides within the bull. 3.4.
Meditation on the Dancing Form:

One-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed; holding a *durdhūraka* flower and the moon in the left hand, with one hand extended toward a peacock feather, and the right leg raised while the other is bent. (p. 13a, f. 2a)

I perpetually worship Naṭeśa, who wears a svastika-shaped earring on his left ear, who holds a hand-drum, the Gaṅgā, and the gesture of fearlessness, whose matted locks are disheveled, and who dwells within the body of Apasmāra;
[this is] the meditation on Kalyāṇasundara. 4. (l. 2)
[He is] the color of vermilion, three-eyed, endowed with four arms, adorned with necklaces and armlets, possessed of divine ornaments,
and beautified by bracelets, anklets, and garlands of *kahlāra* lotuses. The Goddess, with her own hand placed upon his right upper hand, should likewise have two hands raised above.
I bow to the auspicious deity Kalyāṇadeva, who bears a black axe and is accompanied by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
(5) [He is] in the state of wandering for alms and meditation; white in luster, with auspicious eyes, holding a *ḍamaruka* drum and a blade of *dūrvā* grass in his right hands.

I worship the Lord of the Alms-round, who holds a trident and a skull-cup in his left hand, whose feet rest upon excellent sandals, who bears matted locks and wears the moon, who carries a deer in his right hand and a *bhūta* spirit in his left, and who is endowed with the quality of being mounted [upon them]. (2)
The meditation on the enemy of desire:

[one should visualize the deity] whose body is smeared with ashes, who bears the moon, who is adorned with matted locks and a braided topknot, who holds an axe and a black antelope, and who sits pure and firm in the heroic posture. (3)

Placing the palm of his right hand upon his left thigh, I worship the Lord of Smara, who wears a tiger skin as his garment and whose forehead-eye has burnt the supreme Yogi. (4) This is the meditation on Kālāri.

Having visualized [the deity] with the luster of a *bandhūka* flower, possessing three eyes and eight arms, holding a trident in his right hand and a sharp-edged axe (*ṭaṅka*) with excellent fangs in his left, with his forefinger, needle, and noose extended before him,
his left foot slightly bent and raised toward the lotus of the *niṛti* direction, and [trampling] Kāla—
One should meditate upon the Destroyer of Time, who is destroying this entire world and who is praised by the best of sages.
(2) The meditation on Tripurāri: He has three eyes shining upon his broad body, and he holds in his hands an arrow, a black antelope, an axe, and a bow. (3)
With one foot raised and the other well-placed to the right, he was the destroyer of the cities, possessing a gentle smile and a consuming fire.
The meditation on Jālandhara is as follows:
he is red in luster, of fierce gait, and endowed with three eyes; his hands are beautifully adorned with a ṭaṅka, a black antelope, and a plow.
He stands upon the earth, supporting Jālandhara who is rising up, and he possesses the form of the slayer of Karṇaghna and the destroyer of Jālandhara. (10) (p.14b)

Abiding in the lion-posture (gajāri-dhyāna), with his right foot thrust forward and drawn up by the left leg, holding his tail aloft as a protective shield, wielding a trident, a sword, and a flaming jewel in his two hands— (2).
I worship the Lord Gajāri, who holds a skull-topped staff and a noose in his left hands, possesses fangs, has a red complexion, and is accompanied by the Goddess Guhā, who bestows fearlessness.
(3) Meditation on Vīrabhadra.
Blue in appearance, wearing red garments, with a face knit in a frown, possessing flaming hair and three eyes;
holding in his right hands a sword, a staff, a trident, and an axe, and in his left parts a skull-cup, a shield, a bell, a great mace, and likewise a garland of tinkling bells.
May the form of Vīrabhadra, with joints as firm as a lion’s, manifest before me! (12) [The meditation on the half-lion:
On his left side is one who has the luster of coral, wears a crown of the moon, and is adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads.

I bow to the Lord who is half-lion, who is joined with Ṭaṅka and Bhīti, whose forehead is adorned with a crescent moon, who is rich in banners, who has a dark-blue luster on his left side, who is endowed with a crown-mountain, resplendent with yellow garments and other ornaments, bearing the Pāñcajanya conch, and possessing a hand in the boon-granting gesture. 13. (3)
Meditation on Arddhanārīśvara:

Bearing the form of both male and female in his body, with moon-like matted hair and the luster of a reddish-brown axe, wearing a serpent and a tiger-skin garment, with a bull at his forearm and joined by curved feet on the right side. (4)

I bow to Dhūrjaṭinārīśvara, who holds in his left hand a dark blue lotus petal upon his breast, whose lotus-feet are straight and clad in silken garments, and who is resplendent with beautiful golden ornaments and the like. 14.
This is the Kirāta meditation.
With a dark-blue body, two arms, and holding a bow and arrow, with hair adorned by pearls, he stood firmly;
endowed with two beautiful eyes and a large, noble face, he was wide-chested.
Wearing a garment of tigerskin, he had lips as red as lac and ears adorned with flowers. (2)
One should meditate upon the supreme Kirāta, bound at the feet and adorned with foot-ornaments, slightly smiling. 15. (3) The meditation on Kaṅkāla-deva:
[He is] red in luster, with a face like the moon, wearing a crown, and holding a staff-like arm in his left hand.

I worship the eternal god Kaṅkāla, who has three eyes and holds a lute upon his skeleton; who bears a staff in his left hand and a *ḍamaru* drum in his other [right] hand; and who, in his left and right hands respectively, holds an axe and a black deer. 16. (p.16a) (f.5b)
The meditation on Caṇḍeśānugraha:

Three-eyed, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, resembling a crystal gem, holding an axe and a black [serpent], with his left foot hanging down in beauty, resting upon the supreme state (the head of Śiva), and seated upon a lotus pedestal. (2)

17. One should meditate upon the gracious Caṇḍanātha, who stands upon a bull, holds a garland of flowers and saffron along with the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) in his two hands, possesses a beautiful parasol, and is praised by the best of gods, including Caṇḍakaṇṭha;
this is the meditation for removing poison.

I worship Him who is mounted upon a bull, who possesses a dark throat, who is endowed with the boon-granting gesture of fearlessness, who holds a black axe, who bears the crescent moon, who is adorned by serpents, who wears yellow garments, and who has three eyes.
(4) ... [I worship] him who has the luster of a dark cloud. I worship Him who is mounted upon a bull.
His form is that which removes poison; his side is adorned with a parasol and a peacock feather. 18.
The meditation on the Bestower of the Wheel (*cakrapradāna*):
peaceful, three-eyed, four-armed, bearing the moon, and joined by the Goddess in his left [hand].
I meditate upon him who holds a ṭaṅka and an excellent black antelope in his right hand, bestowing the discus;
whose feet hang down on the left side or are in a state of deep sleep; who is honored by the gaze of Viṣṇu; who is endowed with the ritual rules; and who bestows the discus. 19.
The meditation on the propitiation of Vighna:

(3–4) He holds an axe and a black antelope; he is stainless, with his right foot hanging down and his left foot sleeping upon it; he resembles the moon, has three eyes, and bears matted locks as a crest.

Embracing Vighnarāja with his left arm and placing the other [hand] upon his head, I worship that [deity] who, out of affection, bestows grace along with the Daughter of the Mountain, for the propitiation of obstacles. 20.
Meditation on Somāskanda. (p.17a) (f.6b)
The Lord has limbs resembling the moon,
possesses four arms holding a black antelope, an axe, a bracelet, and the gesture of fearlessness,
and is joined by a left foot with a long garland.
Wearing a crown joined with the Moon and accompanied by the son of Śakti; 21.
The meditation on Ekapāda:
bearing a single form, having one foot, and endowed with a trident, a chisel, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness. (3)
I worship Śiva, whose throat is dark blue, who is most terrifying, and whose feet are honored by the world. 22.
Meditation on the Comfortable Posture:
[I worship Him] who is peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, resembling the sun, with the moon as His crest-jewel, and three eyes. (4)

May Maheśa, who rests upon the other foot while leaning on his left lotus-foot with one hand, who holds a trident, a rosary of wild *akṣa* seeds, and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) in his [right] hands as appropriate, and who is joined by Gaurī on his left— may he, seated comfortably, radiate forth from before me! 23.
Meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti:

(2) Having stepped upon the elements with one foot and placed another foot, multiplied [in size], above them, He explains all words for the sages who partake in the portion of the earth that is His own bracelet. (3) [He stands] upon the earth, which is the portion belonging to His own armlet.
May the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrtti, who constantly bears a serpent, a book, and the *mudrā* known as *hutavahakalikā* in his four lotus-like hands—as previously described—shine forth before me. 24.
(4) Meditation on the Emergence from the Liṅga.
One should visualize the Lord with matted locks upon His crest,
His hand resting on His hip, and the dark-hued Kṛṣṇa and the deer at His side;
He holds an axe in His right hand, possesses immeasurable feet, wears a crown, and is accompanied by Brahmā and Acyuta within the sanctum measured according to the prescribed proportions.
The pure and radiant Haṃsa and Kola situated above and below, arising from the Liṅga; (2) on the right,
with a lotus and joined palms at the heart, or holding a rosary in the left hand, with the other hand placed at the heart in añjali-mudrā, accompanied by Acyuta.

Thus, I worship that pair which, within the heart of all pride, consists of the earth and the intermediate space according to the ritual rule, having the form of a pillar of light, and possessing a radiant nature within its belly. 25.
The twenty-five-fold classification of the forms of Maheśa is completed. With the Goddess as his companion, [he composed] the Śrījātakaśiromaṇi, concerning the twelfth house. (p. 18b)

If the lord of the ascendant, Jupiter, or Venus occupies a quadrant (*kendraka*), that son shall be long-lived, wealthy, and a favorite of the king. He whose [ascendant] lord or Jupiter is not in a quadrant or a trine (*koṇa*)—that man of meritorious deeds, having enjoyed various pleasures, shall live for a hundred years free from disease. When [the lord] is situated in its own or exaltation sign and aspected by benefic planets, he will possess fame, prosperity, great enjoyment, and be endowed with physical vigor.

If the lord of the ascendant is weak and conjoined with a dry sign, one will have an emaciated body, a hot temperament, and be constantly beset by laziness. If Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon are conjoined with the sign of the ascendant, and are situated in the ascendant or its quadrants (kendras), the native will be endowed with the marks of royalty. If Rahu is joined with the ascendant and is aspected by Saturn and Mars, and if Saturn’s son (Rahu) is in the Navāṃśa of the ascendant, the person born will be base. [The results for] the second house: If the lord of wealth (the second house) is Jupiter conjoined with a movable sign...
The second house.

If the lord of the second house is conjoined with Mars, he becomes equal to Kubera; or if the lord of wealth is situated in a quadrant (kendrā), and the lord of the eleventh house is in a trine (trikoṇa) from him, conjoined with or aspected by Jupiter and Venus, one should declare a gain of wealth. (2) If the lord of the second house is conjoined with the lord of the eleventh house, or if the lord of the eleventh house has gone to the sign of the lord of the second house, and at that time the lord of the seventh house is in the eighth house, he becomes equal to Kubera. (3) If the lord of the twelfth house is situated in the eleventh house and is conjoined with the lord of the eleventh house, yet is conjoined with or aspected by malefic planets, he remains truly destitute despite the gain of wealth.

When the Moon is situated in the tenth house and conjoined with malefic planets, a man suffers poverty from birth and subsists on alms. When the lord of the second house is situated in the sixth or eighth house, there is loss of wealth;

if Mars and Rāhu are in the eleventh or second house, there is loss of wealth due to royal punishment. If Jupiter is in the eleventh house, Venus in the second house, and their lord is conjoined with the eleventh house, and the twelfth house is joined by a benefic planet— [the native attains prosperity].

One who is fond of wealth due to the root of Dharma—when the Moon is in its own sign, a quadrant, its exaltation, or its Mūlatrikoṇa, and is joined with or aspected by Mercury—if born in a Puṇya Lagna, there is protection of the family and prosperity. (2) When the lord of the second house is in its highest exaltation and is aspected by Jupiter, or likewise even in its own sign or friend's sign, one born [at that time] possesses the power to protect a thousand [people] through his majesty. When the lord of the seventh house is endowed with strength, a man becomes handsome; [this applies when it is not] in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth [house]. (3)

One should predict eye-deficiency from the conjunction [of Jupiter] (4). If Vāgīśa (Jupiter), endowed with its proper configuration and conjoined with a benefic, is in its own division (*varga*) or its own *navāṃśa*, it makes one a master of speech; if conjoined with Guru (Jupiter) (5), one becomes a lord of the world; or if in the *pārāvata* division, or likewise in the *airāvata* division, provided it is not joined by the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) or Mercury, and is in its own exaltation or its own sign, one becomes a lord of wealth.

If Mars is associated with a malefic planet in the second house, or conjoined with a malefic planet, one becomes a speaker of untruths, a slanderer, and afflicted by wind-related diseases. (2) Now, the results for the third house: If Mars is the lord of the third house and is aspected by a malefic, they say there is destruction of siblings; [if it is] aspected by a malefic, there is the loss of siblings.

If [the lord of] the third house is aspected by or conjoined with malefic planets, there will be the cause of the destruction of brothers today; or even if it is conjoined with or aspected by a benefic, there will be the increase of brothers. Or, if the lord of the third house is situated in a quadrant, a trine, its own exaltation, or its sign of friends, or if the lord or the Karaka planet is so placed, there will be the gain of brothers—thus says Budha. If Venus is in the third house and its lord is conjoined with the Moon, while the Karaka is conjoined with Saturn, there will be one sister and one elder brother.
If the Karaka is conjoined with Rahu and the lord of the third house is in a *nīca* (depressed) state...
[text continues].
The Fourth House.

Subsequently, due to the state of being uterine brothers, that [first] would become three; if the lord of the house of brothers (the third house) is a Karaka situated in a quadrant (kendram), or in its trine (trikoṇam), conjoined with Jupiter, or in its exaltation, the number of uterine brothers is twelve. This is the third conception; the first and second [conceptions] are in the seventh and ninth [houses], and the twelfth is the place of death. The remainder is the full lifespan of the uterine brothers; this becomes six conceptions from the Yamala yoga. When Mars is conjoined with the lord of the twelfth house and also conjoined with Jupiter in the house of brothers—

If [Venus] is joined with the Moon, there will be seven brothers; for those who have two [mothers], there is destruction [of one] when Venus is joined with Venus or with Mars. Now, the results of the fourth house: if [the lord of the fourth] is in its own sign, its own Navamsha, its exaltation, or situated in a sign of happiness, there will be an increase in happiness and vehicles.

One should indicate the sounding of conchs, drums, and other musical instruments, as well as walls of various colors and decorated houses. When the lord [of the fifth house] is in a quadrant along with the son [Jupiter], and the lord of the third house is a benefic, aspected by the planet Venus, and Mercury is joined with the ascendant, that man will be honored by his kin. (2) When the third house is joined with a benefic, the significator (Kāraka) is endowed with strength, and its lord is in its sign of exaltation, one should predict long life for the mother. Furthermore, when the lords of Mercury and others are situated in their own signs of exaltation... (3)

If [the lord of the fourth house] is in its own sign, situated in a friendly sign, aspected by a benefic, and conjoined with a benefic, there will be an increase in land for men. If the lord of the fourth house is situated in a quadrant, and Venus and Mercury are in a quadrant from the Moon and in their exaltation signs, he is indeed a wise scholar. [This occurs when] Saturn is devoid of the fourth house.

If Mars has gone to the lot of the Moon and is situated in the house of gain, one obtains gains such as cattle, buffaloes, and the like; however, if it is conjoined with a planet in its sign of debilitation, or if the lord of that sign is in the fourth house, or if Mars is in the sixth or the twelfth house, the man will incur dumbness. If the lord of the eighth house is a benefic, while the lord of the fourth house is in its sign of debilitation and the significator (Kāraka) is in its own sign, he goes from village to village. If the lord of the sixth house is in the fourth house conjoined with the lord of the eighth, and the lord of the fourth house possesses strength, [it brings] [gain] from kinsmen.

In the *Kṛtsita* [chapter]: When the lord of the maternal house is in its own division (*svāṃśa*) or in its own sign (*svārāśi*), one should predict the loss of the mother by casting rays upon that division. (5) If the sign of the lord of the fourth house is occupied by Venus in its state of debilitation (*mūḍha*), there will be no death from the arms of Rāhu, provided it is joined with Jupiter and occupies its exaltation sign.

In the [Dasa] of Mercury and likewise of Venus—when the twentieth or twenty-sixth year is reached—one will obtain a vehicle or eloquence of speech. If the Sun is in the vehicle-sign (the seventh house), and Venus is conjoined with its exaltation or conjoined with the lord of that sign and aspected by Venus, one will obtain a vehicle in the thirty-second year. If the lord of the tenth house is conjoined with the lord of the fourth house and situated in its exaltation degree, and when the forty-second year is reached, it brings the gain of a human vehicle. When the lord of the eleventh house is situated in a sign of happiness (the fourth house) and the lord of the fourth house is conjoined with the eleventh house, [it results in gain] in the twelfth year.

When the fifth house is attained, it bestows the gain of a vehicle drawn by men; this is the nature of the fifth house. If Mercury is in the sign of Saturn in the house of children (the fifth house), and is conjoined with or aspected by Saturn and the others [Mars and Jupiter], then the son himself takes [the paternal wealth]. If the Sun and Moon are situated in one sign and endowed with the same degree, then these two boys have three mothers, while their parents [have only one]. Thus is the fifth house.

(1) However, there are two nourishers: when the fifth house is conjoined with the lord of the sixth, and its lord is situated in the twelfth house, while the lord of the ascendant is weak, one will certainly have a son given to him. (2) When Venus, Jupiter, or Mercury is the lord of the fifth house, and is endowed with strength or aspected [by benefics], they say that one will constantly have many sons throughout his life. (3) This should be considered according to the strength [of the planets] in the fifth house. If the Moon is in the sign of Venus, or if the Sun is situated in the portion of the Moon, a wise man should declare that a daughter will be born at that time.

If Rāhu is conjoined with Saturn in the ninth house and situated in the sign of the Moon, the man born will be devoid of offspring. If the fifth house is conjoined with Rāhu and not aspected by the Moon and Jupiter, the man born will likewise be childless. When the Moon is in the ninth house and not aspected by Jupiter, nor joined with the Moon and Venus, [the same result follows].

If the Moon is joined with Rāhu or Ketu at the time of birth, they declare it to be certain [that there will be no son]. When the Moon is in the twelfth house from the ascendant and Jupiter is in the eighth house from the ascendant, conjoined with or aspected by malefics, there is doubt regarding another [son] being born. If the lord of the fifth house is in its exaltation, situated in a quadrant or a trine from the ascendant, and is conjoined with or aspected by Jupiter, the person attains the fortune of having a son. However, if it is conjoined with three or four malefics and is associated with the lord of the ninth house, [the result is otherwise].

If Jupiter is in the fifth house conjoined with Venus, the person will be a destroyer of his lineage; however, if Jupiter is in the fifth house and its lord is joined with Venus, he will obtain a son. If the lord of the fifth house is in its exaltation sign, one should predict the birth of a son in the thirty-second year. Furthermore, if the lord of the fifth house is situated in the ninth house and is conjoined with the significator (the Sun), one should predict the birth of a son in the twenty-sixth or thirtieth year.

If Jupiter is in the ninth house from the ascendant, the Moon is in the ninth house from Jupiter, and the lord of the ascendant is endowed with strength, one shall obtain [the fruit] in the fortieth year; if Rahu is in the fifth house and its lord is conjoined with malefics, and Jupiter is in its sign of debilitation, there will be the death of a son in the thirty-second year.

If a malefic planet is situated in the fifth house from the *jīva* (the lord of the ascendant), or likewise in the fifth house from the ascendant itself, then in the twenty-sixth, twenty-third, or fortieth year, there will be the loss of a son. If Saturn is conjoined with the lord of the ascendant, and the lord of the ascendant is in its sign of debilitation, then in the fifty-fifth year, one will be overwhelmed by grief for a son. If the fourth house is conjoined with a malefic, the sixth house is likewise endowed with a malefic, and the lord of the fifth house is in its highest exaltation (*paramocca*) yet conjoined with Mars, there will be ten sons. If Jupiter is in its highest exaltation and the lord of the second house is conjoined with Rāhu, and the lord of the ninth house [is likewise situated]...
[as per the fragmentary manuscript].

If Saturn is in the fifth house from the fifth sign (the Lagna), and the lord of that fifth house is also there, one will have nine sons endowed with good fortune; however, if it is a double birth, there will be two sons from two wombs (twins). (2) If Venus is in the fifth house from the second house (the Arudha of wealth), and the lord of the fifth house is also in the fifth, one obtains six sons; but if the fifth house is afflicted by death, there will be only four sons. (3) If Jupiter is in the fifth house from the Ascendant, and the lord of the fifth house is also in the fifth from Jupiter, or if Rahu is in the fifth house from Saturn, one should predict only one son. (4) If the fifth house is conjoined with malefic planets...

If Saturn is in the fifth house from the Guru (Jupiter) and is conjoined with the lord of the seventh house, there will be another wife. If Mars is in the fifth house, the child born from that union will perish; furthermore, the children will not be long-lived. Now, the results of the sixth house.
Next, the sixth house.

If the lord of the sixth house is afflicted by malefic planets, or if the lord of the third, fourth, or seventh house is the ruler of the sixth; if a malefic planet occupies the house of disease (the sixth), and its lord is conjoined with a malefic; if Saturn is conjoined with Rāhu; then the person will always be afflicted by disease. If Mars occupies the house of disease and its lord is conjoined with the eighth house, the man will suffer from fever in the sixth or twelfth year. If Jupiter occupies the house of enemies (the sixth) and is conjoined with the Moon in that same house—

In the twenty-second or nineteenth year, one should predict abdominal disease (*kukṣiroga*), provided Rāhu has gone to the house of disease and is conjoined with Saturn in a quadrant. If the lord of the ascendant is in its sign of debilitation, there is wasting disease in the twenty-sixth year. If the lord of the third house is in the house of disease and its lord is in the twelfth house, one should predict abdominal tumor (*gulmaroga*) in the twenty-third or nineteenth year. If the Moon is in the sixth house and conjoined with Saturn and Mars, one should predict blood-leprosy (*raktakuṣṭha*) in the fifty-second year.

If the lord of the ascendant is situated in the eighth house, and Saturn is conjoined with a malefic, the man will suffer from wind-related diseases in his fifty-ninth year. (2) If the lord of the eighth house is in the sixth house and the lord of the twelfth house is joined with the ascendant, and the Moon is conjoined with malefics, there is danger from wild animals in the eighth year; if Rahu is in the sixth or eighth house, then in the eighth year from that [period], and if Saturn is in the eighth house, there is danger from fire in the third year, and he suffers from the affliction of birds. (3) If the Sun is in the sixth or eighth house and is conjoined with the Moon in that same year, in the fifth or ninth year, [there is danger]. (4) In the fifth or ninth year, [there is danger].

One should indicate fear of shame: when the lord of the fifth house is situated in the sixth house from that [ascendant] sign, and the lord of the sixth house is in the eleventh house; when the lord of the fourth house is situated in the sixth house, and Jupiter is conjoined with the lord of the sixth house; when the lord of the ascendant is in the Vyādha division, his son will become an enemy. When the lord of the ascendant is situated in the sixth house, and the lord of that sign is in the sixth house from it—(p. 26b, f. 8a).

In the tenth and nineteenth years, the fear of the Śoṇaka is declared. Now, regarding the house of the wife (the seventh house): if the lord of the wife is joined with or aspected by a benefic planet, or possesses full strength, [the native] is said to be endowed with good fortune, virtuous, and to enjoy various kinds of fortune such as a wife and so forth. However, if the lord of the wife possesses many virtues due to reasons such as being in its exaltation or retrograde motion, one should know that the man has many wives; otherwise, if it is in its sign of debilitation, there will be enmity.

This loan document was written in the hand of Matubhi Poḍināyakkan; it was recorded at Paikami-mōmanāṭṭai by Śāṣam Govinda.
(p. 29a) (f. 10b) (Tamil script loan document)

This is the debt bond written by Poḍināyakkan of the village of Yēndum, belonging to the district (tūṭi) of Tirukkovalūr. Because of the necessity of [repaying] the debt, I borrowed one hundred and fifteen nāḷ of gold from you at the rate of seven nāḷ per day for each kaṭu of paddy. If you do not deliver it accordingly, I shall release the aforementioned amount from your possession. [Seal/Signature] As agreed upon.
The debt for the white cloth recorded in my mind on this day...
